author: micyoung75
text:
Since Dr. Hotez gave this interview, the numbers have moved. As of May 21: 746 suspected cases and 176 deaths in DRC. An American has been exposed in a healthcare setting in Congo and is being medically evacuated to Germany, along with six high-risk contacts.

The Bundibugyo strain still has no approved vaccine. Two Ebola vaccines exist. Neither covers this one. Hotez said it plainly: if someone funded his team at Texas Children's, they could move into vaccine development. The faster, the better.

The Trump administration announced travel bans on DRC, Uganda, and South Sudan. That is a reactive measure, not a preparedness infrastructure. The global health response capacity that would normally support outbreak containment in conflict zones - the USAID global health programs, the pandemic preparedness offices - has been significantly reduced.

The World Cup arrives in Houston in less than a month. DR Congo plays Portugal at NRG Stadium on June 17. Congolese fans will travel. Some will arrive at Bush Intercontinental feeling ill from causes entirely unrelated to Ebola. Houston hospitals will need management plans for that complexity.

Hotez is not warning of an epidemic in Houston. He is warning that the preparedness questions need answers before the crowds arrive, and that an administration that cut pandemic response infrastructure is not well positioned to provide them quickly.

author: jbthomson51
text:
Ebola outbreak in DRC and Uganda passes 1,000 cases, as Italy reports 2 suspected cases https://t.co/OmgL1bqS0W
[Benjamin Mateus]
With the Ebola toll past 1,000 cases, the gap between the WHO's recommendations and conditions in the eastern DRC has erupted in the torching of two treatment facilities.
-A 2026 analysis by Ruth McCabe and colleagues at Imperial College London estimated that true infections during the early weeks exceeded official counts by a factor of two or more.
-The socioeconomic baseline of the region exposes the structural inequality of global capitalism. Life expectancy is 62.5 years, well below the African average and decades below that of the United States. An estimated 72.3 percent of the population survives on less than $2.15 a day. Maternal and child mortality are staggering: 76 under-five deaths per 1,000 live births and 846 maternal deaths per 100,000.
Set against the trillions in mineral wealth extracted from the region by multinational corporations, these figures expose the WHO’s “low” global risk assessment as both shortsighted and false. Recurrent Ebola outbreaks and the emergence of other deadly pathogens will threaten millions, regionally and globally, as long as these conditions persist. The demographic and social collapse in the eastern DRC is no natural phenomenon but the deliberate product of imperialism and capitalist exploitation—what Friedrich Engels called social murder.
